idiom_name: service classes that publish operations, own transactions and delegate domain logic
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define one application service per subject area and expose its operations as the application's boundary; each operation starts or joins the transaction, loads the aggregates through repositories or gateways, delegates every decision to domain objects, stores the changes, coordinates the response (notifications, messages, event publication) and commits - an exception rolls the whole operation back. The two classical shapes are the domain facade (thin service methods that only orchestrate a rich Domain Model) and the operation script (thicker service methods that implement the application logic themselves while still delegating domain logic to the model); where several services share gateways and helpers, a Layer Supertype carries the common collaborators. Keep the layer thin and the operation set stable: clients bind to the boundary, and a service that starts to contain business rules is a signal to push them back into the model.
code_sketch:
# operation script (thick) vs domain facade (thin)
class OrderService:                       # application boundary, one per subject area
    def place(self, req):
        with unit_of_work() as tx:        # transaction owned here
            order = self.orders.load(req.customer_id)      # gateway
            order.reserve(req.items)                       # domain logic
            self.orders.save(order)
            self.mail.send_confirmation(order)             # response coordination
            tx.commit()

class BillingService:                     # domain facade: no logic of its own
    def statement(self, customer_id):
        return Customer.load(customer_id).statement()
pitfalls: Skipping the boundary for one client (a script, an admin console) so the same operation is enforced differently depending on the entry point.
Letting the service accumulate domain rules until the model is anemic and the service is a transaction script with better naming.
Opening the transaction in the UI or in a repository instead of at the operation boundary, which produces partial writes and competing owners.

Wrong move: annotating an internal helper as transactional and calling it via this.helper() from another method of the same service -> in proxy mode (Spring's default) the call never passes through the proxy, so no transaction starts and its rollback rules silently do not apply -> invoke through the injected bean/proxy, move the operation into a separate service, or switch to weaving mode when every call must be intercepted.

Wrong move: relying on default rollback rules when the operation throws a checked or declared exception -> Spring-style declarative transactions roll back only on RuntimeException/Error by default, so partial work is committed and the caller receives a 'successful' failure -> declare rollbackFor (or the global rollback-on-all-exceptions setting) for the business exception types, or translate them into unchecked application errors at the boundary.

Wrong move: calling a remote system (payment gateway, HTTP API, mail server) while the operation's transaction is still open -> the slow or hanging call pins database connections and row locks, so a third-party latency spike becomes an application-wide outage -> commit the local state first and publish the notification afterwards, or record the intent in an outbox row inside the transaction and let a background process deliver it after commit.
